q: What is the Altdorfer landscape Sotheby’s is selling in December 2026?
a:
A landscape by Albrecht Altdorfer of about 1520, unknown to scholars until it surfaced in a Swiss private collection. Sotheby’s offers it in its Old Masters Evening Sale in London on 9 December 2026, estimated at £3m–5m.

It is one of three known oil landscapes by Altdorfer. The other two are in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich and the National Gallery in London. No Altdorfer has been offered since 1980, when the National Gallery paid £2.4m for *Christ Taking Leave of His Mother*.

It is on view in New York from 7 to 19 November and in London from 4 to 9 December.

q: When is Art Basel Miami Beach 2026 and how large is it?
a:
Art Basel Miami Beach runs **4–6 December 2026** at the Miami Beach Convention Center, with VIP days on **2–3 December** (Art Basel).

- **272 exhibitors** from more than 40 countries and territories; 204 in the main Galleries sector.
- First-time countries: the Bahamas, Estonia, Georgia, Ghana and Hungary.
- The floor is reconfigured: about 12% less space, about 10% fewer Galleries exhibitors, four hospitality plazas instead of five.

**Read.** A smaller fair after a soft New York week. The cut in floor space is the organiser’s own signal that dealers are spending less on booths.

q: What did Art Basel offer dealers after Art Basel Paris closed early in October 2026?
a:
**A 20% cut in stand fees for every exhibitor.** Art Basel offered it to all 211 exhibitors of Art Basel Paris (The Art Newspaper, 11 November). It is a discount on fees, not a cash payment.

**Why.** The fair ran at the Grand Palais from 20 October. It closed two days early, on 23 October, because of rioting in Paris. By The Art Newspaper’s count it ran about three and a half days of the five and a half planned, about 36% short. Smaller dealers on the upper floor lost most: they rely on the weekend.

**The dealers.** The Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) speaks for 57 of the exhibitors. Its letter to the fair director, Karim Crippa, accused the organiser of “disrespect, even contempt” and asked for concrete proposals. Its president, Philippe Charpentier, says 20% is the rate the committee expected.

**Art Basel.** Its chief executive, Noah Horowitz, stands by the decision to close and says MCH is fully committed to the 2027 edition. He did not comment on insurance or on the Grand Palais.

The reading: a fair can now lose its weekend to events in the street, and the organiser, not the insurer, has absorbed the first cost.

q: What are the Artnet and Kalshi art prediction markets?
a:
**Betting on sale results, settled on auction data.** On 11 November Artnet became the official art partner of Kalshi, a prediction market and exchange. Kalshi lists yes-or-no contracts on auction results, fairs and other art events. Traders buy and sell them peer to peer. Artnet’s Price Database supplies the verified results that settle them. Artnet News has no part in setting the markets or checking the results.

Markets on the New York November sales are already trading. Markets on Miami Art Week in December are due later in November. The report gives no volumes and names no lot.

Why it matters for the desk: the odds on a lot are a public, priced view of the outcome, set before the hammer. A guarantee is a private one. Watch whether the two diverge on the Van Gogh, the Kandinsky and the Klimt.

q: What does ArtTactic’s September 2026 confidence survey say about the contemporary market?
a:
ArtTactic’s Contemporary Art Market Confidence Report of September 2026 put overall confidence at 56, slightly optimistic, up from 43 in March 2026.

- Auction-market confidence: 78, up from 69.
- Primary-market confidence: 51, up from 45.
- 60% of the experts surveyed expect sales to stay flat over the next six months.

The caution is history. The index fell from 75 in February 2022 to 42 that July, and from 54 in January 2025 to 30 six months later. Optimism has twice faded within half a year. New York’s contemporary sales of 16–19 November are the next test.

q: What is Bonhams’s Brancusi: The Legacy sale in November 2026?
a:
**The sale.** Five bronzes by Constantin Brâncuși, offered by Bonhams in New York on 18 November as a single-owner sale, expected to make about $25m together.

**Provenance.** Fresh to market: held privately for decades after being acquired from the artist’s estate (USA Art News).

**Context.** The bronzes are most of Bonhams’s November New York expectation of at least $40m. They are shown in the Steinway Hall rotunda of Bonhams’s new flagship at 111 West 57th Street, opened in 2026. In May, Christie’s sold Brâncuși’s *Danaïde* for $107.6m, his auction record.
src: The Art Newspaper: the week’s preview

q: Did Bonhams’s Brancusi: The Legacy sale on 18 November 2026 sell, and for how much?
a:
**Reported, not confirmed.** Bonhams had published no result for *Brancusi: The Legacy* by 23 November that the desk could read.

**What is reported.** Curatorial.ro reports that all five bronzes sold for about $15.1m together, against a combined estimate of about $25m. It does not say whether the prices include the premium. It also says Bonhams then described the lots as moved to private sale with confidential results. Treat every figure here as reported.
- *Torse de jeune homme*: about $4.2m (posthumous cast, 1991, edition of 8).
- *La jeune fille sophistiquée*: about $3.4m against $3.5–5.5m (posthumous cast, 1973, edition of 5).
- *Tête abstraite (Tête de femme)*: about $2.8m against $3–5m (posthumous cast, 1980).
- *La Muse endormie II*: about $2.8m (posthumous cast, 1981, edition of 8).
- *Tortue*: about $1.9m against $2–4m (posthumous cast, 1982, edition of 5).

**Why it matters.** All five are reported as posthumous casts. That sets them apart from the lifetime *Danaïde* that made Brâncuși’s $107.6m record at Christie’s in May 2026. A result below estimate fits a market that pays for rarity and condition, not for a name alone.

q: How are US tariffs hurting the Canadian art market?
a:
Since 22 August 2026 the United States has charged a 50% tariff on a wide range of Canadian imports. It covers paintings, drawings, sculpture, prints and collages. Most other art still enters the US free: the Section 301 regime exempts works of art, antiques and collectibles.

Canadian dealers are losing their American buyers.
- Equinox Gallery puts US buyers at about 15% of its sales and expects that share to fall to zero.
- Macaulay & Co says US buyers made up about 10% of its sales of Lawrence Paul Yuxweluptun’s work.
- Macaulay & Co has cancelled a fair during Miami Art Week in December: “it’s just too risky”.

Dealers are turning to Europe and Australia instead. The Art Dealers Association of Canada argues that Canadian art “is not simply another category of merchandise”.
src: The Art Newspaper: tariffs exempt art

q: What is the full estimate of Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale in New York on 17 November 2026?
a:
**$550.9–797.8m without premium, for 79 lots.** HENI totals the low and high estimates of every lot; none is at estimate on request. It is the largest evening sale of the week on paper, ahead of Sotheby’s Blaquier-Arrieta collection (about $450m, as reported).

**Guarantees.** 29 of the 79 lots are guaranteed (HENI), about 37% by number. HENI does not split them between Christie’s and third parties. The Kandinsky carries a third-party guarantee; the Klimt is guaranteed.

**The five largest lots.**

| Lot | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Kandinsky, *Betonte Ecken* (1923) | $60–80m, guaranteed |
| Klimt, *Litzlbergkeller* (1915) | $60–80m, guaranteed |
| Picasso, *Le Baiser* (1969) | $40–60m |
| Picasso, *Tête de femme (Dora Maar)* (1941) | $25–35m |
| Giacometti, *Figure, demie grandeur (no. 2)* | $20–30m |

The two Picassos come from Jeff Koons’s own collection. The sale starts at 6.30pm ET (Oliver Shuttleworth).

**How to read it.** The low estimate is the bar. A guaranteed lot that hammers at its low estimate to one bidder may have gone to its guarantor. So judge the sale on the hammer against $550.9m and on how many guaranteed lots drew more than one bidder. [[sale:christies-20c-new-york|The sale]].

q: How did Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale in New York on 17 November 2026 go?
a:
**$626.6m with premium; $521m at hammer**, at the low end of a $511–743m estimate after withdrawals (Artsy, Artlyst). HENI had counted $550.9–797.8m for 79 lots before them.

**The top lots.**
- Wassily Kandinsky, Betonte Ecken (1922–23): $85.8m ($74m hammer) against $60–80m; three bidders, opening at $54m; his record, nearly double the $44.8m of 2023.
- Gustav Klimt, Litzlbergkeller (1915–16): $82.3m ($71m hammer) against $60–80m.
- Pablo Picasso, Le Baiser (1969), from Jeff Koons: $31.1m ($26.5m hammer) against $40–60m. Koons paid $17.4m in 2008.
- Alberto Giacometti, Figure, demi-grandeur (no. 2): $25.9m ($22m hammer), sold without reserve.

**The collections.** Koons’s seven lots made about $104m, all guaranteed by Christie’s. The William I. Koch collection made $66.3m, with Diego Rivera at $9.9m against a $3.5m high estimate.

**The misses.** Calder, Stella and a Frida Kahlo were withdrawn, the Kahlo over export issues. Seven small Pollocks, a Modigliani portrait and a Léger went unsold. De Kooning, Ryman and Hockney sold below their low estimates.

**Records.** Six, among them Kandinsky, Cornelis van Haarlem ($13.9m), Wifredo Lam ($11.6m) and Botero ($5.2m).

q: How did Christie’s 21st Century Evening Sale in New York on 19 November 2026 go?
a:
**$145.9m with premium, $117.7m at hammer.** The pre-sale estimate was $126–192m without premium, so the sale landed **below** its low estimate at hammer (The Art Newspaper). It closed the New York week.

**The lots.** 56 offered; five failed to sell, a 9% buy-in rate. Two were withdrawn, among them a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated at $3–5m.

**The guarantees.** 24 lots carried third-party guarantees and nine house guarantees, about 59% of the works offered.

**The top lots.**
- Jean-Michel Basquiat, *Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads)* (1983): $32.8m ($28m hammer) against $30–50m, to a telephone bidder. Below the low estimate.
- Andy Warhol, *Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle)* (1962): $9m ($7.3m hammer) against $6–8m.
- Roy Lichtenstein, *Large Spool* (1963): $8.6m ($7m hammer) against $10–15m; third-party guaranteed.
- Vija Celmins, *Untitled (Ocean)* (1990): $7.1m ($5.7m hammer) against $6–8m; third-party guaranteed.
- Gerhard Richter, *Abstraktes Bild* (1990), from the late Marian Goodman: stalled at $5.7m against $6–8m and did not sell.

**The collections.** The ten Agnes Gund lots made $25.7m ($20.3m hammer), within $16–24m. The 19 lots from Antonio Homem Sonnabend made $41.9m ($33.3m hammer), below $35–55m.

**Records.** Jim Nutt, *Loom* (1999), $1m ($850,000 hammer), more than double its $350,000 high estimate; Julia Jo, *One Fell Swoop* (2026), $409,600; and Antonio Santín, *Trampolín* (2025), $486,400 (Artsy).

**What it tells us.** The most guaranteed sale of the week was the weakest against its estimate. Guarantees placed the lots; they did not lift them. Christie’s evening sales for the week made $772m, down 5% on last year (USA Art News).
src: The Art Newspaper: a tepid 21st Century sale

q: What did Yoshitomo Nara’s In the Milky Lake / Thinking One make at Fair Warning in November 2026?
a:
**$15.9m.** Loïc Gouzer’s Fair Warning sold Nara’s *In the Milky Lake / Thinking One* (2011) on 19 November 2026 in New York, against an estimate of $10–15m (USA Art News). The report does not say whether $15.9m includes the premium, and no hammer is published, so the desk gives no verdict against the estimate.

**The bidding.** Four bidders, from the United States and the Middle East. An American buyer won, according to a source familiar with the sale.

**Not a record.** It is Nara’s third-highest auction price. His record is $24.9m for *Knife Behind Back* (2000) at Sotheby’s Hong Kong in 2019.

**Context.** USA Art News calls it the highest price for a living artist’s work in the week. The work had been private since it was made.

q: What is the Hedreen collection that Sotheby’s is selling in November 2026, and why is it being sold?
a:
**The collection.** Richard Hedreen, 91, is a Seattle developer whose firm owns the Grand Hyatt and other downtown hotels. About 50 of his works go to Sotheby’s from 16 November, among them works by Titian, Willem de Kooning and Roy Lichtenstein.

**The estimates.** The works are estimated at $109–158m or more (Seattle Times). The leaders are Lichtenstein’s *Reflections on "Painter and Model"* (1990) at $20–30m, lot 4A of The Now and Contemporary Evening Auction on 16 November; de Kooning’s *Water…Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII)* at $20–30m; and Sam Francis’s *Towards Disappearance* at $15–20m.

**Why it is sold.** At least 18 of the works are collateral for a loan. A Bank of America loan of 2025, replacing a Goldman Sachs loan of 2012, is secured on about 44 major works; the paper estimates it at over $100m, unconfirmed. The sale repays the loan. The collection had been pledged to Seattle University for a planned museum. The 2024 announcement called it a $300m gift, but it was a pledge, and the $25m of "seed funding" was a de Kooning sold privately for a reported $17m. Hedreen has committed the remaining 350 or so works to the university, with no timeline.

**For the Read.** This is a lender’s sale, not a collector’s choice: the consignor needs the money. Watch whether the Lichtenstein draws bidders beyond the estimate.

q: What is the Hilma af Klint painting at Bukowskis in November 2026, and could it set a record?
a:
**Very likely, if it sells.** Bukowskis offers *Ser III No. 5* (January 1920), oil and graphite on canvas, 38.5 by 29 cm, in Stockholm on 19 November. The estimate is SEK 6–8m, about US$600,000–800,000 (The Art Newspaper).

The af Klint auction record is **$165,825**, for the watercolour *The Power of the Spleen* (1931), at Stockholms Auktionsverk in 2019. The low estimate is more than three times that. Only two of her abstract paintings have sold at auction before, both more than 30 years ago.

**Provenance.** The Hilma af Klint Foundation deaccessioned the work in 1995. One private collector has owned it since. Af Klint made 85 works in a few months in early 1920.

**Context.** Her watercolour *Vid ankdammen* (1910) made £40,640 at Christie’s in March 2026 against £6,000–8,000. A painting by an artist with almost no auction history is a test of museum fame turning into price: her 2018 Guggenheim show drew more than 600,000 visitors. [[sale:bukowskis-af-klint|The sale]].

q: What did Hilma af Klint’s Ser III No. 5 make at Bukowskis on 19 November 2026?
a:
**SEK 128.9m, about $12.7m.** Bukowskis sold *Ser III No. 5* (1920) at its Modern Art & Design sale in Stockholm on 19 November 2026. The hammer was SEK 108m (Sweden Herald). The estimate was SEK 6–8m, so the hammer landed far **above** it: the final price is about 16 times the high estimate (Hyperallergic).

**Records.** Bukowskis calls it the most expensive work of art ever sold at auction in the Nordic countries. It beats af Klint’s previous auction record of $165,825 (Stockholms Auktionsverk, 2019) many times over.

**The work.** Oil and graphite on canvas, 38.5 × 29 cm. The Hilma af Klint Foundation deaccessioned it in 1995; one private collector held it since. Only two other abstract paintings by her have sold at auction, both more than 30 years ago.

**The buyer.** Not named. Bukowskis gave no details of the bidding.

**What it tells us.** Scarcity beat caution. A museum-famous name, almost never offered, at a modest estimate, drew a price that no guarantee set.

q: Is Italy setting up a panel for Nazi-looted art?
a:
A bill introduced in March 2026 by Federico Mollicone (Brothers of Italy) would let the government create a five-member committee to rule on claims for art seized or sold under duress between 1933 and 1945. It would have to decide within 180 days of a claim, and the government would have six months to set the system up. The bill is before the lower house’s culture committee.

A 2001 inquiry counted 7,847 seizure warrants issued up to April 1945. Four publicly known disputed works hang in Italian museums, among them Manet’s *Portrait de M. Arnaud à cheval* (1875) at Milan’s Galleria d’Arte Moderna.

q: How much did the Kalshi prediction markets trade on the November 2026 New York auctions, and were they right?
a:
The Art Journal (Jeni Fulton, 20 November 2026) counted **58 single-lot markets** on the Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Phillips New York sales. They traded **$635,860 over 7,127 trades**. Kalshi counts each contract at its $1 payout, so the cash staked was lower; Kalshi does not publish it.

- The **Van Gogh** *Châtaigniers en fleurs* was the most-traded lot: $97,886, about 15% of the total. On 11 November traders gave a 58% chance of clearing $200m. It made $190.4m with fees ($165m hammer). The house’s estimate of about $180m was closer.
- The **Basquiat** *Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads)*: traders gave an 80% chance of beating $35m. It made $32.9m with fees ($28m hammer).
- A single basketball market ($125,153) traded more than all Phillips lots together ($104,216).
- The 53 markets settled on Artnet’s data traded $490,274.
- By Artnet’s count, 64.2% of the seven evening sales’ estimated value was guaranteed.

**Read.** The crowd was more bullish than the houses on the two top lots and wrong both times. The volumes are too small to move a guarantor or tempt an insider.
src: The Art Journal: Bet the lot

q: How did Christie’s MAWASIM sale in Abu Dhabi on 1 November 2026 go: the estimate, the guarantees, the records and the result?
a:
**$8.94m with premium.** MAWASIM: 20 Years of Modern and Contemporary Middle Eastern Art was Christie’s first fine-art auction in Abu Dhabi. It made $8,940,800 with premium. USA Art News reports 60 of 68 lots sold; the catalogue listed 70 works by 58 artists from 13 countries.

**Estimate and guarantees.** Christie’s published no total estimate and no hammer total, and none of the reports mentions a guarantee or an irrevocable bid. So the sale has no verdict against its estimate. Christie’s calls it its best result for the category since 2015.

**The top lots.**
- Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian, *Variations on the Hexagon* (2006): $844,800 against $150,000–250,000, after nearly seven minutes of bidding.
- Fahrelnissa Zeid, *Composition* (1948–49): $524,800.
- Faisel Laibi Sahi, *Baghdad Café* (2016) and Ali Banisadr, *Homo Deus* (2018): $512,000 each.
- Paul Guiragossian, *Noces*; Mahmoud Saïd, *Portrait de Princesse Fadia*; Zeid, *Endless Thoughts*: $486,400 each.

The top ten made $4.72m, 52.8% of the total.

**The nine records need parsing.** On Christie’s own classification, three are artist records (Jellal Ben Abdallah, $204,800; Faisel Laibi Sahi, $512,000; Juliana Seraphim, $83,200). Two are records for a medium (Guiragossian; Samia Halaby, *Yesterday*, $358,400). Four are auction debuts (Nabil Kanso, Rami Farook, Fatma Lootah, Afra Al Dhaheri). Art in Context notes that the Halaby medium record sits awkwardly with a £400,000 oil on canvas sold in 2020.

**The bidders.** Christie’s says 37% of registrants were new to the house and over 30% were millennials or Gen Z. These are registrations, not buyers.

**What it tells us.** The house is building a market ahead of demand. The works came from established Gulf and Levantine collections (Dalloul, Trad, Barjeel). Artprice puts Middle East auction sales down 28% for the year to June 2026. Sotheby’s first Abu Dhabi fine-art sale follows on 10 December.

q: What has changed in the New York November 2026 sales since the line-up was announced?
a:
A week before the sales, the line-up has filled out. The changes since 2 November:

| Sale | Date | What is new |
|---|---|---|
| Phillips, Modern & Contemporary Evening | 17 Nov, 4pm ET | Phillips’s own page gives 17 November, not 18. Beyond Every Art reports a Hockney, *David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982*, at $10–15m; Phillips’s page names only the Modigliani *Tête* ($28–35m). |
| Sotheby’s, The Now and Contemporary | 16 Nov, 7pm ET | Nine named lots, $64–94m without premium on the desk’s sum: the Lichtenstein ($20–30m), the Kusama and the Bacon ($10–15m each), Cecily Brown ($7–10m), Nara ($5–7m), de Kooning ($4.5–6.5m), and Warhol’s *Flowers*, Bradford’s *If Caught Outside* and Frankenthaler’s *Black Touch* ($2.5–3.5m each). |
| Sotheby’s, Modern Evening | 18 Nov, 7pm ET | Hopper’s *The Martha McKeen of Wellfleet* ($20–30m) and, as reported by Beyond Every Art, Signac’s *Collioure. Les Balancelles (Opus 167)* ($12–18m). |
| Sotheby’s, Blaquier-Arrieta | 18 Nov, 6pm ET | Sotheby’s lists the Van Gogh and the Cézanne at estimate on request. The $180m and $120m figures are the ones given to the press, not published estimates. |

ArtCollectorNews reports that Christie’s expects more than $800m of material in its marquee week. At Sotheby’s premium rates, Beyond Every Art puts the Lichtenstein at $23.7–35.2m to the buyer.

The tests are unchanged. Watch the guaranteed Van Gogh, Kandinsky and Klimt for bidders above the guarantee, and the Kusama after a Kusama failed in London in October. [[sale:sothebys-blaquier-arrieta|The Blaquier-Arrieta sale]] is the week’s centre.
src: Beyond Every Art: dates and estimates

q: How did the New York evening sales of 16–18 November 2026 go?
a:
Records at the top, thin bidding beneath them. Totals include premium; verdicts are from the hammer.

| Date | Sale | Total | Hammer | Estimate | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 Nov | Sotheby’s: the Baum collection | $109.9m | $90.8m | $74.4–109m | within; 24 of 24 sold |
| 16 Nov | Sotheby’s: The Now and Contemporary | $268.7m | $224.78m | $226.2–323.1m | below, by $1.4m |
| 17 Nov | Christie’s: 20th Century | $626.6m | $521m | $511–743m | within, at the low end |
| 17 Nov | Phillips: Modern & Contemporary | $104.4m | $85.75m | $69.9–98.8m (reported) | within; 20 of 21 sold |
| 18 Nov | Sotheby’s: Blaquier-Arrieta | $412m | $358m | about $450m | below; 12 of 12 sold |
| 18 Nov | Sotheby’s: Modern | $365.8m | $305.21m | $260.2–378.4m | within |

**The records.** Van Gogh, $190.4m ($165m hammer), bought by William Acquavella in the room. Kandinsky, $85.8m ($74m hammer), after three bidders. Kusama, $15m. Cassatt, $13.3m. Aaron Douglas, $14.48m.

**The shortfalls.** The Van Gogh hammered below its guide of about $180m. The Cézanne Arlequin made $111m ($99m hammer) against about $120m. Six of the twelve Blaquier-Arrieta lots sold below their low estimates. The Koons collection’s Picasso Le Baiser made $31.1m against $40–60m.

**What it tells us.** The guarantees found buyers, but often a single one. Contested lots (the Kandinsky, Phillips’s Modigliani, the Magritte at $45.5m) are the evidence of demand. Bonhams’s results of 18 November were not found by the desk.
src: The Art Newspaper: the Fischer settlement

q: How much do the auction houses expect from New York’s November 2026 sales?
a:
**The total.** The four houses expect at least $2.04bn and possibly more than $2.4bn (The Art Newspaper, 12 November). All figures are before buyer’s premium unless stated.

**By house.**
- **Sotheby’s:** more than $1.1bn, a house record for a marquee season. About 40% is the Blaquier-Arrieta collection (12 works, about $450m, fully guaranteed).
- **Christie’s:** $823m–1.1bn. The 20th Century Evening Sale on 17 November is estimated at $550.9–797.8m (HENI), led by Kandinsky and Klimt at $60–80m each. The 21st Century sale is led by a Basquiat at $30–50m.
- **Phillips:** $80.4–128.7m, led by Modigliani’s limestone *Tête* at $28–35m.
- **Bonhams:** at least $40m, most of it from five Brâncuși bronzes expected to make about $25m together.

**The theme.** Single-owner collections carry the week: Blaquier-Arrieta, Baum, Hedreen and Armand Hammer at Sotheby’s; Jeff Koons, Agnes Gund, Clive Davis and William Koch at Christie’s.
src: The Art Newspaper: the week’s preview

q: What did the New York November 2026 auction week make in total, by house?
a:
**About $2.44bn, up from $2.23bn a year earlier** (USA Art News, 21 November).

**Evening sales.** About $2.03bn, up 7% from $1.9bn, against a combined low estimate of $1.7bn. Day sales added $406.1m. USA Art News’s house figures sum to about $2.07bn, slightly more than its own evening total; it does not explain the gap.
- Sotheby’s: $1.2bn in evening sales from 136 lots, up 18%, plus $157.1m in day sales.
- Christie’s: $772m in evening sales from 130 lots, down 5%, plus $225.6m in day sales.
- Phillips: $104.4m from 22 lots, up 55% from $67.3m, plus $23.4m in day sales.
- Bonhams: not reported.

**Other counts.** Seoul Economic Daily gives about $2.41bn for 15 sales of 16–20 November, with Sotheby’s at $1.31bn, its highest weekly total, and Christie’s at $967m with sales still to come. The figures differ by basis and by which sales are counted.

**Records.** Artsy counts 20 artist records, led by Van Gogh ($190.4m) and Kandinsky ($85.8m), with Sam Francis, Kusama, Aaron Douglas, Cornelis van Haarlem and Wifredo Lam.

**The read.** The total rose on a few very expensive lots. Against estimates the week was weaker: the Blaquier-Arrieta collection hammered $56.5m below its low estimate, and Christie’s 21st Century sale missed its low.
src: The Art Newspaper: a tepid 21st Century sale

q: How did Phillips’s New York evening sale of 17 November 2026 go?
a:
**$104.4m with premium; $85.75m at hammer**, up 55% on last year’s $67.3m. USA Art News reports an aggregate estimate of $69.9–98.8m, so the hammer landed within it.

**The lots.** 22 were offered; Derek Fordjour’s Haberdasher was withdrawn and only Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia went unsold, at $500,000. Fourteen lots were guaranteed (The Art Newspaper).

- Amedeo Modigliani, Tête (1911–12): $44.6m ($38.2m hammer) against $28–35m, after a ten-minute, three-way contest.
- David Hockney, David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982: $12.2m ($10m hammer), within $10–15m.
- Alexander Calder, Snow Flurry, May 14 (1959): $7.5m, above its high estimate, one of the few lots without a third-party guarantee.
- Pollock and Stella sold below their estimates.

**What it tells us.** A smaller Phillips, with fewer lots and a profitability goal, did better than a year ago. Its best lot drew three bidders.

q: Is Phillips pulling back from competing with Christie’s and Sotheby’s?
a:
**Yes, by its own account.** Chief executive Martin Wilson says Phillips no longer intends to grow at all costs; it is "time really to look at profitability" (a syndicated report of 16 November).

**The evidence.** This week Phillips’s two top lots are estimated above $10m, against 45 such lots at Christie’s and Sotheby’s together. Former executives say the owners, Leonid Fridlyand and Leonid Strunin of Mercury Group (owners since 2012), grew reluctant to make large guarantees. Phillips reportedly stepped back from the $922m Macklowe collection, which Sotheby’s won. Jonathan Crockett resigned as chairman of Phillips Asia in September.

**The numbers.** Phillips sold a record $746m of art and design in 2022. Bonhams beat it in reported sales last year by $43m. Phillips still leads watch auctions: a Geneva sale this month made $112.3m. Phillips expects $80.4–128.7m from its November New York sales.

**For the Read.** Fewer guarantors at the top leaves the trophy market to two houses, which concentrates guarantee risk on them.

q: What is the French fraud investigation into Picasso plates and medallions?
a:
A criminal investigation is open in Aix-en-Provence into silver plates and gold medallions sold as Picasso designs. Paloma Ruiz-Picasso filed the complaint on 10 March 2026 for the nine heirs. It alleges fraud, counterfeiting, forgery and concealment. No one is named, and the investigation is at a preliminary stage.

The objects are linked to Ateliers Hugo, the Aix goldsmith. The complaint says its moulds were reused for unauthorised editions, duplicates and unnumbered pieces. The Picasso Administration counts at least 17 suspect collections, hundreds of pieces in all.

The trail through the salerooms:
- Sotheby’s London sold a set of 24 silver plates for £1.4m in October 2021. The seller was the dealer Mark Maurice. The Museum of Old and New Art in Tasmania first raised doubts.
- Bonhams Paris postponed a sale of 95 Ateliers Hugo lots in 2023, two days before it, after the Picasso Administration called them unauthorised. Estimates ran from €400 to €50,000 a lot.
- In November 2023 Bonhams declined a set of 24 plates estimated at £900,000.

Pierre Hugo died in October 2023, and his five children declined the inheritance; his heirs reportedly face a €2.5m tax debt. For Picasso multiples, the Administration’s view now matters as much as the edition number.

q: What did the Paris court decide on the Flavian heirs’ Pissarro claim against Sotheby’s?
a:
**Restitution ordered.** On 5 November 2026 a Paris court cancelled Sotheby’s London sale of 25 June 2024 and ordered the painting returned at once to the heirs of Salomon Flavian. The work is Camille Pissarro’s *Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne* (1902), a view of the port of Dieppe. It sold for £1.2m.

**The reasoning.** The court found that the painting was looted in Paris in 1941. It found “no direct and convincing evidence” of the claimed pre-war sale to Edward Le Bas through Paul Rosenberg. Sotheby’s argued that a French court has no jurisdiction over a London sale. The court held that, under French law, annulling the 1941 dispossession voids every later sale.

**What else it decided.**
- Sotheby’s must disclose the buyer’s “complete identity” within two months, with a penalty of €1,000 a day for delay.
- All claims against Sotheby’s itself were dismissed.
- The agreement between Mondex and two of the seven heirs, who waived their rights shortly before the sale for a share of the price, stands.

**What comes next.** Mondex intends to appeal. Sotheby’s is considering whether to join the appeal, and says enforcement in the UK will need its own procedure. The heirs’ lawyer, Corinne Hershkovitch, calls it “a very important ruling”.

**Why it matters.** A French court has voided a London sale. The risk on a work with a wartime gap in its provenance now follows the work across borders, even when the auction house is cleared.

q: How did the Gotha museum get its lost Rubens sketches back?
a:
Five oil sketches by Peter Paul Rubens are together again at the Ducal Museum in Gotha, for the first time in more than 80 years. Rubens painted them on panel in 1620–21 as studies for the ceiling paintings of the Jesuit church in Antwerp.

Three left Gotha at the end of the Second World War. Representatives of the ducal family took them to Coburg as American and Soviet forces closed in, and they were sold illicitly. Two others were taken by the Red Army and returned to Gotha in 1959.

The recoveries:
- *St Gregory of Nazianzus* came back in 2024 from a museum in Buffalo, New York, with Christie’s help.
- *The Prophet Elijah in the Golden Chariot* came back in 2026 from a private American collection, in a private settlement mediated by Cabinet Turquin and paid for by the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation. Its secretary general, Martin Hoernes, says a “figure in the low millions” was agreed, below market price. The price is reported, not published.
- *St Augustine* belongs to the Foundation E. G. Bührle Collection, which has lent it for the exhibition.

A wartime gap is often closed by a negotiated price rather than a court.

q: How did Shanghai art week go in November 2026?
a:
**The fairs.** West Bund Art & Design (13th edition, 85 galleries, 10–15 November) and Art021 (14th edition, 111 galleries) opened in the same week, against slower economic growth.

**The mood.** The Art Newspaper calls the Chinese market at an "all-time low", but the city lively. Speculative buyers have gone; collectors take longer over expensive works; younger collectors favour artists of their own generation.

**Reported sales.** Thaddaeus Ropac sold Megan Rooney’s *That Sky (Atlas)* (2026) for a reported £400,000 to a Chinese foundation, and a Martha Jungwirth for €200,000. Hauser & Wirth sold Louise Bourgeois’s *Point of Contact* for $450,000 to a Kuala Lumpur museum and a George Condo for $200,000. Art021 launched an acquisition initiative with LACMA for Asian and Asian-diaspora artists.

q: What is in Sotheby’s first Abu Dhabi fine-art sale, Breaking Ground, on 10 December 2026?
a:
Breaking Ground is Sotheby’s first international fine-art auction in Abu Dhabi. It is held on 10 December 2026 at the Saadiyat Grove Experience Centre on Saadiyat Island. It closes Collectors’ Week: the exhibitions open on 4 December and the luxury sales are on 9 December. No total estimate is published.

The named lots:
- Claude Monet, *Prunes et Abricots* (1882–85): $2–2.6m (The National).
- Andy Warhol, *Ads* portfolio (1985): $2–3m (Sotheby’s).
- Jadé Fadojutimi, *Untitled* (2022): $500,000–700,000.
- Fernando Botero, *Donna con Ombrello*, bronze (2008): $350,000–550,000.
- Christo, *The Mastaba of Abu Dhabi (Project for United Arab Emirates)* (2007): $180,000–250,000.
- Etel Adnan and May Muzaffar, *Ta’ir al-Nar (Firebird)* (1998): $50,000–70,000.
- Najat Makki, *A Woman’s State of Being* (1988): $30,000–50,000.

Works by Mohamed Ahmed Ibrahim, Hassan Sharif, S. H. Raza and Paul Guiragossian are also offered.

It follows Christie’s first Abu Dhabi sale, MAWASIM, which made $8.94m with premium on 1 November. The Fadojutimi is a small test: Fadojutimi was among the young artists who failed or sold far below estimate at Sotheby’s London in October.

q: Break down Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening Auction on 16 Nov 2026: the estimate, the guarantees, the lots to watch. What does it tell us?
a:
**When.** Monday 16 November, 7pm ET, an hour after the Baum collection sale.

**The estimate.** Sotheby’s has not published a total. The nine named lots sum to $64–94m without premium (the desk’s sum). Sotheby’s expects more than $1.1bn across its November New York sales.

**The lots to watch.**
- Roy Lichtenstein, *Reflections on "Painter and Model"* (1990), $20–30m, lot 4A, from the Hedreen collection.
- Francis Bacon, *Self-Portrait*, $10–15m.
- Yayoi Kusama, *No. 3P.B.*, $10–15m.
- Cecily Brown, *Untitled (Shipwreck)*, $7–10m.
- Yoshitomo Nara, *Candy Blue Night*, $5–7m.
- Mark Bradford, *If Caught Outside*, $2.5–3.5m.

**The guarantees.** Not yet disclosed. The desk could not tell from Sotheby’s digital catalogue or the Lichtenstein’s lot page which lots carry a guarantee or an irrevocable bid, and the press previews of 12 November give no count. The guarantee symbols usually appear in the printed catalogue and the saleroom notices; the desk will add them with the result.

**What it tells us.** The sale tests contemporary demand after London. In October Sotheby’s London contemporary sale missed its low estimate at hammer and a Kusama sold for a quarter of its low estimate. A $10–15m Kusama in New York is the cleanest test of whether that was London or the market. The Lichtenstein is a lender’s sale: the Hedreen works are sold to repay a bank loan.

q: Break down Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening Auction on 16 Nov 2026: the estimate, the guarantees, the lots to watch and the result. What does it tell us?
a:
**The estimate.** $226.2–323.1m for 53 lots, without premium (The Art Newspaper).

**The result.** $268.7m with premium, $224.78m at hammer: just under the low estimate. The Art Newspaper counts two lots withdrawn and five unsold, so 46 of 51 sold. USA Art News counts three withdrawn and 45 sold. About 45% of lots hammered within estimate.

**The guarantees.** Sotheby’s has published no count of guarantees or irrevocable bids. USA Art News reports that guarantors were outbid on 29 of the 45 lots it counts as sold. The desk could not confirm that figure from Sotheby’s.

**The lots.**
- Roy Lichtenstein, Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990), the first Hedreen lot: $24.6m ($22m hammer), within $20–30m.
- Yayoi Kusama, No. 3P.B. (1960): $15m ($12.5m hammer), within $10–15m; her auction record.
- Sam Francis, Towards Disappearance I (1958): $17.1m ($15m hammer), at the low end of $15–20m; his record (reported among the night’s lots by The Art Newspaper).
- Records too for Jonas Wood, Tomma Abts and Firelei Báez.

**What it tells us.** London in October was not the whole market. A Kusama that might have repeated October’s collapse set a record instead, and guarantors were frequently outbid. But the sale still missed its low estimate at hammer: buyers paid for the best works and not for the rest.

q: What is Turner’s Rome, From Mount Aventine and what is it expected to make at Sotheby’s in December 2026?
a:
**J.M.W. Turner, *Rome, From Mount Aventine*, 1836.** Sotheby’s offers it in its Old Masters and 19th-century evening auction in London on **9 December 2026**. The estimate is about **£50m**; some reports say more than £50m (The Art Newspaper; PA).

- It last sold at Sotheby’s London in **2014 for £30.3m** with fees. That is still Turner’s auction record, so the estimate alone would beat it (The Art Newspaper).
- The 5th Earl of Rosebery bought it in 1878. It has changed hands once since and is in a private collection. The consignor is not named.
- It has never been relined or restored; Turner’s fingerprints and palette-knife marks are visible (PA).
- Sotheby’s showed it in Rome in late September and shows it in London from 3 to 9 December.
- No guarantee has been published.

**Read.** After a New York week in which the top lots sold at or under their guides, the Turner tests whether a top estimate holds for a fresh, unrestored masterpiece. A sale near £50m at hammer would support the desk’s view that the rare thing at a defensible guide still finds depth.

q: What is the restitution claim on Sotheby’s Van Gogh, Châtaigniers en fleurs, in November 2026?
a:
**The claim.** Heirs of the German Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer have asked Sotheby’s to withdraw Van Gogh’s *Châtaigniers en fleurs* (1890) from the Blaquier-Arrieta sale on 18 November. Their lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, wrote on 12 November that unless Sotheby’s shows the 1936 sale was at market value and would have happened without Nazi-era pressure, "no auction may take place". The heirs cite the Reich flight tax the family had to pay.

**The provenance.** Samuel Fischer bought the picture in 1909. After his death in 1934 it passed to his family. It was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933, and in 1936 it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris (Sotheby’s provenance, as reported by the BBC). The Times of Israel names the dealer Walter Feilchenfeldt as the seller. The Blaquier-Arrieta family bought it in 1975.

**Sotheby’s position.** Sotheby’s says its research "to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress" and that it is "committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution". The heirs say they will seek a fair and just solution under the 1998 Washington Principles, which are not binding.

**Why it matters.** The lot is estimated at about $180m and guaranteed by Sotheby’s, so the house bears the risk if bidders stay away. A syndicated report says experts fear the dispute could deter buyers and that a settlement may not remove the risk of further claims. As of 15 November Sotheby’s had not said whether the lot stays in the sale.
src: The Art Newspaper: the week’s preview

q: How was the Fischer heirs’ claim on the Blaquier-Arrieta Van Gogh resolved?
a:
By a private settlement, hours before the sale. On 17 November Sotheby’s announced an agreement between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer. Neither side has released the terms or said whether the heirs will be paid.

**The claim.** The Fischers bought Châtaigniers en fleurs (May 1890) in 1909. It was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 and sold to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936, three months after the family left Berlin. On 12 November the researcher Gunnar Schnabel asked Sotheby’s, for the heirs, to show the sale was at market value and to delay the auction.

**The outcome.** The sale went ahead on 18 November. The painting made $190.4m ($165m hammer), the Van Gogh auction record, below its guide of about $180m hammer.

**The lesson.** A guaranteed lot with a late provenance challenge was settled rather than withdrawn. The cost of the settlement, whatever it was, falls outside the published price.

q: Why are galleries closing in Vienna?
a:
In November 2026 The Art Newspaper reported that four galleries are closing or leaving Vienna. Exile is closing after 18 years and Zeller van Almsick after nearly ten. Emanuel Layr is closing his gallery for a project-based model with a smaller space by appointment. Eva Presenhuber, who opened in Vienna in 2022, is leaving the city.

The reasons given are rising costs and an unpredictable market. It is the primary market’s side of the split: auction confidence is up, the middle of the gallery trade is still thinning.
